title: Symphony No. 3 in C minor, “Organ”
hook: Saint-Saëns said he gave this symphony everything he had; the organ waits almost ten minutes for its first note.

painting.title: The Organ Rehearsal
painting.collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
painting.pairingNote: Painted in Paris the year before the symphony, a singer rehearsing beside the organ in a church loft; Saint-Saëns had spent more than twenty years as an organist in Paris churches.

facts: The Philharmonic Society of London asked Saint-Saëns for a new work, and he wrote the symphony in the first months of 1886, at the same time as his comic *Carnival of the Animals*. He conducted the premiere himself at St James’s Hall, London, on 19 May 1886; in the first half of the same concert he played Beethoven’s Fourth Piano Concerto.
He meant to dedicate it to Franz Liszt, his friend and supporter. Liszt died in July 1886, and the score was published “to the memory of Franz Liszt”.

Saint-Saëns wrote the symphony in two movements, each in two parts, and said it still “contains, in principle, the four traditional movements”. This recording, like many, gives the four parts as four tracks, and they follow each other with hardly a break.

The organ plays in only two of the four parts, and there is a piano too, sometimes played by two pianists at once. One theme runs through the whole work and keeps changing character, a method Saint-Saëns learned from Liszt. Some hear the opening notes of the chant [[dies-irae|Dies irae]] in it; others think the likeness is chance.
“I gave everything to it I was able to give,” Saint-Saëns said. “What I have here accomplished, I will never achieve again.” He never wrote another symphony.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a sighing introduction and restless strings (I), a calm hymn over the organ (II), a fierce scherzo with flashing piano (III), the organ’s blazing C major finale (IV).

movements.heading: Adagio – Allegro moderato
movements.summary: A short, slow introduction of sighing woodwind phrases, then a restless, nervous Allegro. The quick, repeated notes in the strings are the symphony’s main theme, and they will come back in many disguises. The movement does not end: it fades away into the slow movement that follows.

mainIdeas.name: The main theme
mainIdeas.description: quick, nervous repeated notes in the strings, turning around a few notes like a worried thought.

mainIdeas.name: The second theme
mainIdeas.description: a smoother, singing melody that brings some calm.

stops.hear: Slow and quiet: soft string chords, and short, sighing phrases in the oboe and other woodwinds
Quick, nervous repeated notes in the strings; the woodwinds’ sighs gather into a melody above them
stops.happening: *Allegro moderato*. The restless string figure is the main theme of the whole symphony

stops.hear: Calmer: a smooth, singing melody
The nervous theme returns, louder, and is worked over, with brass calls cutting through
The restless opening music returns in the strings
The singing melody again, then the music starts to lose energy
stops.happening: The movement begins to wind down

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Very quiet: plucked cellos and basses, slower and slower, settle on a single low note
stops.happening: The bridge into the *Poco adagio*, which follows without a break

notice: Learn the nervous string figure at ≈ 0:55. In the finale it returns as a slow, majestic hymn.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Charles Munch recorded the symphony with the Boston Symphony Orchestra in Symphony Hall, Boston, in April 1959, with Berj Zamkochian at the hall’s organ. On the Spotify album the symphony is tracks 1–4, followed by Debussy’s *La mer* and Ibert’s *Escales*.

movements.heading: Poco adagio
movements.summary: The organ enters for the first time, on a single soft note, and the strings sing a long, calm hymn over it. This is the slow movement of the symphony, though Saint-Saëns joined it to the first. It is warm and still, and it fades into silence at the end.

mainIdeas.name: The hymn
mainIdeas.description: a slow, broad melody for the strings in [[unison|unison]], over quiet held chords on the organ.

stops.hear: A single soft, low note on the organ, then a warm chord
stops.happening: The organ’s first entry, opening a new key, D-flat major

stops.hear: The strings, all on one line, sing a slow, broad melody over the organ’s quiet chords
The melody again in an unusual blend of colours: clarinet, horns and trombones spread over three octaves, with the strings now holding the chords
Organ and strings answer each other; the plucked basses recall a scrap of the restless first theme
The violins sing the hymn again, fuller and more richly decorated
The organ changes colour to a shimmering, slightly wavering sound, with a very deep bass that is felt more than heard

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The music fades away to nothing

notice: The organ plays its first note almost ten minutes into the symphony, and it is very quiet. Saint-Saëns saves its full power for the finale.

movements.heading: Allegro moderato – Presto
movements.summary: Part Two opens with a fierce, stamping [[scherzo|scherzo]] in C minor. Twice it gives way to a brilliant *Presto* in C major, where the piano adds glittering scales. Then the energy drains away into a quiet, searching passage that prepares the finale.

mainIdeas.name: The scherzo
mainIdeas.description: an aggressive, stamping figure in the strings, a hardened form of the main theme.

mainIdeas.name: The *Presto*
mainIdeas.description: fast, light music in C major, with rushing scales on the piano.

stops.hear: A fierce, stamping figure in the strings, with timpani
Suddenly bright and fast: rushing strings and woodwinds, and the piano adds glittering scales
stops.happening: The *Presto*, in C major, in the place of a [[trio|trio]]

stops.hear: The fierce scherzo music returns
The bright *Presto* again, more briefly
The music grows quiet; the strings pass a slower form of the main theme between them, as if searching
stops.happening: A transition that prepares the finale

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Hushed and expectant
stops.happening: It leads straight into the finale

notice: In the *Presto*, listen for the piano’s quick scales, up and down the keyboard. They sound like sparks thrown off by the orchestra.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The two pianists are Bernard Zighera and Leo Litwin.

movements.heading: Maestoso – Allegro
movements.summary: A huge C major chord on the full organ opens the finale. The restless theme of the first movement has become a broad, triumphant hymn, sung by strings and organ with brass fanfares. After a busy, fugue-like passage and a brief pastoral moment, the music builds to a long, blazing ending.

mainIdeas.name: The hymn
mainIdeas.description: the symphony’s main theme, now slow, broad and in C major.

stops.hear: A huge C major chord on the organ, and the orchestra answers
stops.happening: *Maestoso*. The organ’s full power, for the first time

stops.hear: The strings play the main theme as a broad hymn while the piano ripples high above
stops.happening: The theme as a [[chorale|chorale]], with piano for [[four-hands|four hands]]

stops.hear: Organ and strings play the hymn together at full volume, with brass fanfares between the phrases
stops.happening: The grand statement of the theme

stops.hear: Faster and busier: the strings set off one after another on a quick tune
stops.happening: *Allegro*; a [[fugato|fugato]] on a faster form of the theme

stops.hear: A quieter moment with gentle woodwind melodies
The music gathers strength again
The main theme returns at full power, organ and full orchestra

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: Massive chords; the organ’s bass slides down a C major scale, and a long final chord holds

notice: Compare the hymn at ≈ 0:20 with the nervous string figure at the start of the first movement. It is the same theme, slowed down and turned from minor to major.

threads.title: One theme, many faces
threads.body: The restless figure of the first movement returns as the stamping scherzo and finally as the finale’s hymn. Saint-Saëns learned this [[thematic-transformation|thematic transformation]] from Liszt, the symphony’s dedicatee.

threads.title: Dark to light
threads.body: The symphony moves from C minor to C major, the same path as Beethoven’s Fifth.

threads.title: The organ held back
threads.body: Silent for the first ten minutes, then soft and hushed, the organ is kept for the moment the finale begins.

threads.title: Four in two
threads.body: Saint-Saëns joined his four movements in two pairs: the first fades into the slow movement, the scherzo grows into the finale.
